data.title: GE Vernova (GEV) Can Win across the Power Bottleneck

data.title: McDonald's Uses AI to Set Big Mac Prices Across U.S. Stores as Franchisees Face Rising Local Costs
data.description:
McDonald's (MCD) is using artificial intelligence to guide menu prices across its U.S. restaurants and some global locations. The automated pricing tool reads data from millions of daily customer orders to find what McDonald's company reports call the best price for every menu item.

The system relies on software built with Tiger Analytics to check local demand for McDonald's. Calculating how much local buyers in specific neighborhoods want to spend helps the computer make custom price suggestions for each McDonald's store location.

The AI Software Has Created Price Gaps in its Items among McDonald's Stores

The AI pricing software has created bigger price gaps between nearby McDonald's stores. Price checks show that a McDonald's-owned store in Fresno, California, sells a Big Mac for $5.69, while another McDonald's store two miles away sells the same sandwich for $6.89.

Screenshots of the pricing screen show messages that rank McDonald's store price sensitivity. To create its price picks, the computer also pulls public prices directly from online menus at nearby competitor stores like Wendy's (WEN) and Burger King. Both rival chains stated that they do not use computer programs to pick menu prices.

McDonald's Is Allowing Store Owners to Set Their Own Final Prices

McDonald's states that store owners are free to set their own final prices. However, several McDonald's store owners report feeling pressure from McDonald's management to use the computer price picks. Internal records show that McDonald's corporate systems track every time a store owner strays from the suggested price.

In January, McDonald's updated its business rules to require McDonald's store owners to work with approved pricing advisers and tools. Friction exists because McDonald's corporate headquarters makes money from a percentage of total store sales, while McDonald's store owners must pay rising local bills for rent and worker pay, which is up 36% since 2019.

Pricing Computer Programs Are Facing Growing Checks from the Government

The expanded push into computer pricing creates legal and public image risks for McDonald's. Legal terms inside the pricing tool warn McDonald's store owners that because local franchisees act as business rivals, using shared software tools could draw attention from market regulators.

Former Federal Trade Commission leaders note that pricing computer programs face growing checks from government officials over market price-fixing worries. McDonald's stated that its pricing portal serves as an informational tool to help store owners make good business choices rather than a required pricing rule.

Is McDonald's a Good Stock to Buy?

McDonald's stock has a consensus Moderate Buy rating among 25 Wall Street analysts. That rating is based on 15 Buys, 10 Holds, and one Sell recommendation issued in the past three months. The average 12-month MCD price target of $297.96 implies 28.8% upside from current levels. data.title: RTX Stock (RTX) Falls Flat Despite Missile Contracts Firing Up Growth Hopes
data.description:
Shares in defense group RTX (RTX) were flat-footed today despite landing a new multi-billion-dollar missile contract and a prediction of surging future growth from a leading analyst.

Missile Interceptor Demand

RTX said that its Raytheon subsidiary had secured the five-year contract, with two additional years available as an option, worth up to $24.4 billion for the supply of Standard Missile-6 or SM-6, interceptors.  

"SM-6's multi-mission capability is vital to our customer, and Raytheon is intensely focused on meeting the demand," said Raytheon President Phil Jasper. "By continuously investing in our operations and facilities, we are removing constraints and boosting capacity to ensure we deliver this critical capability our sailors depend on."
The order is expected to ensure a steady supply for the US Navy and significantly increase the availability of these missiles, which can conduct offensive strikes and missile defense missions.

Raytheon said it has expanded its workforce, partnerships with the defense industry and production automation in order to increase its capacity. The SM-6 can perform air defense, anti-ship warfare and ballistic missile defense missions.

data.title: Fox Stock (NASDAQ:FOXA) Notches Up as Warner Takes Aim at Dating Show
data.description:
Media giant Fox (FOXA) just ran afoul of what is about to be one of the biggest new media conglomerates around, as Warner Bros. Discovery (WBD) took aim at Fox over a new dating show that Fox is planning known as The Vow. Apparently, The Vow is way too much like The Bachelor for comfort, and Warner has issued a cease-and-desist letter accordingly. Fox investors, meanwhile, liked the controversy, and gave shares a fractional boost in Friday morning's trading. Fox has seen a 1.1% loss in its share price over the past year.

Way Too Many Similarities for Warner's Liking

The cease-and-desist letter that Warner sent out includes several instances of "allegedly infringing material," according to a report from the Hollywood Reporter. Falling rose petals are involved, along with an image of a man wearing a tuxedo and holding a rose. The words "the bachelor" appear, and the show's host is revealed as Chris Harrison, who was also former host of The Bachelor.

Warner's letter spells it out in very heavy legal terms, saying: "Taken together, the above represents a plain attempt to capitalize on and 'ride on the coattails' of WB's instantly recognizable intellectual property and the Franchise's goodwill in violation of, inter alia, state and federal trademark, copyright, and unfair competition laws. Without having seen the Series itself, we cannot comment on it and reserve all rights in connection therewith."

The single-anchor morning show will be replaced with a new version of Big Money, using a roundtable format featuring an entire group of anchors.

The new show will be called Big Money in the Morning, which brings together Dagen McDowell, Brian Brenberg, Taylor Riggs, and Josh Schafer. McDowell and Brenberg will be obliged to end their evening show, The Bottom Line, which will be replaced by reruns of Larry Kudlow's show. This idea should work for a little while, but the more Fox Business has to turn to reruns to fill its roster, the worse off it is in the long run.

data.title: Why Micron and Sandisk Stocks Are Slipping Today (October 2) — and What Wall Street Sees Ahead
data.description:
Micron (NASDAQ:MU) and Sandisk (NASDAQ:SNDK) are moving lower Friday, losing about 2% and 3%, respectively, as memory investors appear disappointed by Micron's muted reaction to its latest earnings. MU delivered huge growth and strong guidance this week, yet its shares struggled to climb afterward, raising concerns that stellar results may no longer be enough to keep the memory rally going. That matters after Micron gained 497% over the past year, while SanDisk soared 1,340%, making profit-taking easier to justify after the muted response.

Micron's Earnings Put the Rally to a Tough Test

Micron offered investors another set of huge numbers this week, yet its share price struggled to follow them upward. Fiscal fourth-quarter revenue reached $54.23 billion, compared with $11.32 billion one year earlier, while adjusted earnings came in at $33.42 per share. The company also projected fiscal first-quarter sales between $60 billion and $63 billion, alongside adjusted EPS ranging from $37.15 to $39.15.

That muted stock reaction could matter more than it initially appears. Investors holding gains approaching 500% just watched Micron deliver tremendous growth without receiving another large move upward afterward. When spectacular financial results stop generating equally strong market reactions, taking some money off the table becomes an easier decision.

data.title: ServiceNow vs. Microsoft: Run Away From One Software Stock, Embrace the Other, Says Investor
data.description:
Enterprise software is going through a period of reassessment as investors weigh the impact of AI on everything from employee productivity to cloud computing and software spending. Some companies might be benefiting from rising demand for AI infrastructure, but others are having to demonstrate that their existing software businesses can continue growing as customers rethink how they use technology.

That makes ServiceNow (NYSE:NOW) and Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) an interesting comparison. The former remains one of the leading names in enterprise software, with strong growth despite the broader pressure on the sector, while the latter combines its enormous software business with Azure, one of the world's largest cloud platforms.

Investor Gary Alexander has been reassessing the two companies and argues that investors need to look beyond headline growth and examine what is actually driving that growth, how much customers are committing to future spending, and whether earnings are keeping pace with valuations.

ServiceNow has held up relatively well during the software sell-off, the shares falling only around 10% since the start of the year, and climbing by 65% since bottoming out in April. The company's resilience reflects continued demand for its enterprise platform, but the rebound has also left investors paying a substantial premium for that growth.

The latest results showed revenue rising 24% year over year to $3.99 billion, beating Wall Street expectations of $3.93 billion. Subscription revenue grew 23% on a constant-currency basis, accelerating from the previous quarter, while ServiceNow slightly increased its full-year revenue guidance.

The headline numbers, however, do not tell the whole story. The company completed its $7.75 billion acquisition of cybersecurity company Armis in April, and Alexander believes the deal contributed meaningfully to the acceleration in reported subscription growth. Armis had previously disclosed annual recurring revenue of $340 million, which implies roughly $85 million of quarterly revenue when simply divided across four quarters. That would represent around three percentage points of ServiceNow's subscription growth in the latest quarter.

The problem is that ServiceNow does not separately disclose organic and acquired growth, making it difficult to determine how much of the acceleration is coming from the underlying business. Alexander also points to remaining performance obligations, which are growing at roughly 21.5% on a constant-currency basis. That is broadly in line with revenue growth rather than running substantially ahead of it.

Profitability presents another question. ServiceNow added around 700 employees during the quarter, taking its workforce to approximately 30,500, up 12% year over year. Its adjusted operating margin consequently remained at 29.5%, giving Alexander limited evidence of the margin expansion that could help support its premium valuation.

Meanwhile, its valuation looks particularly demanding from an earnings perspective: at more than 30 times forward earnings, ServiceNow trades at roughly twice the P/E multiples of software peers such as Salesforce and Workday.

"In my view, ServiceNow's gains are all in the rearview mirror," Alexander summed up. "This company is becoming a souring bet as acquisitions dominate its growth story, while the company isn't making sufficient margin progress to be able to rationalize its valuation multiples down closer to its peers."

"Sell this stock and invest elsewhere," the investor concluded. (To watch Alexander's track record, click here)

Turning to Microsoft, its latest results give Alexander plenty to consider. Revenue rose 17% year over year to $90 billion, while adjusted EPS climbed 23% to $4.74. Azure was the standout, with growth accelerating to 43%, while remaining performance obligations jumped 84% to $678 billion.

The bigger question is what those numbers say about Microsoft's enormous AI spending. So far, the company is showing that its investment in computing capacity can be monetized quickly. Microsoft says demand continues to exceed available capacity, meaning new infrastructure is being absorbed by customers rather than sitting idle while the company waits for AI demand to develop.

Alexander believes that gives Microsoft an important advantage. Azure also has the advantage of sitting on top of Microsoft's huge existing software and cloud business, rather than having to build a new revenue stream from scratch. Microsoft can therefore use its established businesses to support its AI investments while Azure provides an important source of growth.

There are still risks to mull over. AI safety concerns could slow development, Microsoft's exposure to OpenAI creates additional uncertainty, and AI-driven workforce reductions could eventually affect demand for software subscriptions. Commercial bookings have also been uneven. But with Azure growth accelerating and demand still exceeding capacity, Alexander sees evidence that Microsoft's AI investments are beginning to translate into a more powerful growth engine.

Lastly, the valuation is also worth considering. Microsoft trades at roughly 26 times forward earnings, compared with more than 30 times for ServiceNow. "I continue to see more tailwinds than headwinds for Microsoft as Azure growth takes off," the investor summed up. "Stay long here: a mid-20s P/E multiple still leaves plenty of room for upside when accelerating growth is expected ahead."

Accordingly, Alexander rates MSFT a Buy.

Turning now to the Street's view, we find that both are popular choices boasting Strong Buy consensus ratings. NOW's average price target lands at $143.41, offering 12-month returns of a modest 6%. MSFT's $575.91 average target points to one-year gains of 12%. (See NOW stock forecast or MSFT stock forecast)

data.title: Why Is the Stock Market Up Today, 10/2/26?
data.description:
Both the S&P 500 (SPX) and the Nasdaq 100 (NDX) are trading higher on Friday with gains of 1.04% and 1.56%, respectively. Falling rate hike expectations at the October 28 Fed meeting are supporting the two indexes, with the odds dropping to 20.5% from 24.4% a day ago, according to the CME FedWatch tool.

Easing Treasury yields are also driving the market higher. The 10-year yield is down 1.8 basis points to 5.21%, while the 30-year is off 3.1 bps to 5.57%.

Rate Hike Odds and Yields Ease After Weak September Jobs Report

Rate hike odds and yields eased after the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) published September's jobs report this morning. The report showed that nonfarm payrolls increased by 29,000 in September, undercutting the estimate of 84,000. In addition, the unemployment rate climbed to 4.2% from 4.1%, above expectations of 4.1%.

data.title: McDonald's Stock (MCD) Looks Like a Buy after the Dip
data.description:
McDonald's (MCD) stock's current dip looks increasingly attractive, and I see MCD as a Buy. For a mature, low-beta business known for steady cash flow, this kind of sell-off is unusual. MCD rarely offers investors many dramatic entry points, but the setup looks very different after it fell more than 30% from its peak earlier this year.

The recent sell-off reflects real and plausible concerns. Affordability remains the biggest problem for the fast-food bellwether, and glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) drugs add a new long-term risk. Still, most of the current pressure looks more cyclical than structural. At the same time, the drop makes MCD much cheaper and pushes the dividend yield higher. NEXT also gives management a clear plan to improve restaurant economics and recover traffic.

data.title: Top Five Biggest Video Game Stock Stories This Week, 10/2/2026
data.description:
It was another busy week for the video game sector. Big titles got new tech, while major companies rolled out new plans and denied rumors. Gamers also saw the release of new games and remasters.

1. The Witcher 3 Gets a Huge New Update

CD Projekt (OTGLY) rolled out a big new update for The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt. The patch adds new gameplay and fresh visual changes. It also brings path tracing and DLSS 4.5 to the game. The update also drove more use of Nvidia's (NVDA) GeForce NOW cloud game service.

2. Gears of War: E-Day Enters Early Access

Microsoft (MSFT) launched Gears of War: E-Day in early access on Oct. 1. It is the first main Gears of War game in seven years. The game is set to get its full launch on Oct. 6. Early feedback has praised its use of RTX tools.

Infinity Ward shared more details on the PC build of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4. The game will have wide-screen support, HDR, and Dolby Vision. Ray tracing will also work in all modes. The new engine can also apply some updates in the background without a full game restart.

4. Dragon's Dogma 2 Heads to Switch 2

Capcom (CCOEF) is bringing Dragon's Dogma 2: Dark Arisen to Nintendo (NTDOF)'s Switch 2 on October 9, 2026. The game will bring its large fantasy world to the new console and joins a packed run of fall game launches. This port comes a little over two years after the game's initial release on Sony's (SONY) PlayStation, Microsoft's Xbox consoles, and PC.

5. Xbox Says It Is Not for Sale

Microsoft pushed back on fresh rumors about an Xbox sale this week. Xbox CEO Asha Sharma said the gaming unit is not for sale. The comment came as Microsoft continues to reshape its game business as part of a larger reset. The statement adds more clarity at a time when Xbox is making major changes across its teams.
